events.label: Holmes says he must go to Dartmoor and King's Pyland

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I shall have to go. To Dartmoor; to King's Pyland.

events.label: Holmes and Watson discuss Holmes's departure

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Go! Where to?

events.label: Watson agrees to go with Holmes and Holmes invites him to do so

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My dear Watson, you would confer a great favour upon me by coming. And I think that your time will not be misspent, for there are points about the case which promise to make it an absolutely unique one. We have, I think, just time to catch our train at Paddington, and I will go further into the matter upon our journey. You would oblige me by bringing with you your very excellent field-glass.

events.label: Holmes and Watson depart by train for Exeter
Holmes reads fresh papers during the train journey
Holmes speaks about the train's speed and calculates it from telegraph posts

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We are going well. Our rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour. Nor have I. But the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart, and the calculation is a simple one.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson whether he has looked into the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I presume that you have looked into this matter of the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze?

events.label: Holmes explains how he will approach the case

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is one of those cases where the art of the reasoner should be used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of fresh evidence. The tragedy has been so uncommon, so complete and of such personal importance to so many people, that we are suffering from a plethora of surmise, conjecture, and hypothesis. The difficulty is to detach the framework of fact—of absolute undeniable fact—from the embellishments of theorists and reporters. Then, having established ourselves upon this sound basis, it is our duty to see what inferences may be drawn and what are the special points upon which the whole mystery turns.

events.label: Holmes receives telegrams from Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory inviting his cooperation
Holmes says Silver Blaze is from the Isonomy stock and has a brilliant record

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Silver Blaze is from the Isonomy stock, and holds as brilliant a record as his famous ancestor.

events.label: Holmes says Silver Blaze is in his fifth year and has won prizes for Colonel Ross

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: He is now in his fifth year, and has brought in turn each of the prizes of the turf to Colonel Ross, his fortunate owner.

events.label: Holmes says Silver Blaze is the first favourite for the Wessex Cup

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Up to the time of the catastrophe he was the first favourite for the Wessex Cup, the betting being three to one on him.

events.label: Holmes says many people had an interest in preventing Silver Blaze from appearing

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is obvious, therefore, that there were many people who had the strongest interest in preventing Silver Blaze from being there at the fall of the flag next Tuesday.

events.label: Holmes says the danger was appreciated at King's Pyland and precautions were taken

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The fact was, of course, appreciated at King's Pyland. Every precaution was taken to guard the favourite.

events.label: Holmes says John Straker was a retired jockey and served Colonel Ross

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The trainer, John Straker, is a retired jockey who rode in Colonel Ross's colours before he became too heavy for the weighing-chair. He has served the Colonel for five years as jockey and for seven as trainer, and has always shown himself to be a zealous and honest servant.

events.label: Holmes says the establishment had three lads and four horses

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Under him were three lads; for the establishment was a small one, containing only four horses in all. One of these lads sat up each night in the stable, while the others slept in the loft. All three bore excellent characters.

events.label: Holmes says John Straker lived in a small villa with a maid-servant

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: John Straker, who is a married man, lived in a small villa about two hundred yards from the stables. He has no children, keeps one maid-servant, and is comfortably off.

events.label: Holmes describes the lonely country, the villas, Tavistock, Mapleton, and roaming gypsies

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The country round is very lonely, but about half a mile to the north there is a small cluster of villas built by a Tavistock contractor for the use of invalids and others who may wish to enjoy the pure Dartmoor air. Tavistock itself lies two miles to the west, while across the moor, also about two miles distant, is the larger training establishment of Mapleton, which belongs to Lord Backwater, and is managed by Silas Brown. In every other direction the moor is a complete wilderness, inhabited only by a few roaming gypsies.

events.label: Holmes says the general situation was as it was last Monday night when the catastrophe occurred

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Such was the general situation last Monday night when the catastrophe occurred.

events.label: The horses are exercised and watered and the stables are locked up
Two lads walk to the trainer's house and have supper in the kitchen while Ned Hunter remains on guard
Edith Baxter carries supper down to the stables
Edith Baxter carries a lantern on the dark path across the moor
A man appears out of the darkness and stops Edith Baxter
The man steps into the lantern light and is seen to carry a heavy stick and wear a grey tweed suit, a cloth cap, and gaiters
The man asks Edith Baxter where he is and says he had nearly decided to sleep on the moor

communicates.speaker: unnamed_man
communicates.content: Tell me where I am? I had almost made up my mind to sleep on the moor, when I saw the light of your lantern.

events.label: Edith Baxter says the man is close to the King's Pyland training-stables

communicates.speaker: edith_baxter
communicates.content: You are close to the King's Pyland training-stables.

events.label: The man says he understands that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night and asks for the boy's supper

communicates.speaker: unnamed_man
communicates.content: I understand that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night. Perhaps that is his supper which you are carrying to him.

events.label: The man takes a folded white paper from his waistcoat pocket and offers it to Edith Baxter for the boy

communicates.speaker: unnamed_man
communicates.content: See that the boy has this to-night, and you shall have the prettiest frock that money can buy.

events.label: Edith Baxter runs past the man to the meal window
Edith Baxter finds the window already opened and sees Ned Hunter seated inside
Edith Baxter begins to tell Ned Hunter what happened while the stranger comes up again
The stranger greets them at the window

communicates.speaker: unnamed_man
communicates.content: Good-evening.

events.label: The stranger makes a business proposal and mentions the Wessex Cup horses Silver Blaze and Bayard and the weights

communicates.speaker: unnamed_man
communicates.content: It's business that may put something into your pocket. You've two horses in for the Wessex Cup—Silver Blaze and Bayard. Let me have the straight tip and you won't be a loser. Is it a fact that at the weights Bayard could give the other a hundred yards in five furlongs, and that the stable have put their money on him?

events.label: Ned Hunter springs up and rushes across the stable to unloose the dog
The stranger leans through the window and then disappears before Hunter returns with the hound
Watson asks whether the stable-boy left the door unlocked after running out with the dog

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Did the stable-boy, when he ran out with the dog, leave the door unlocked behind him?

events.label: The boy locks the door before leaving it
Hunter sends a message to the trainer and reports what happened

communicates.speaker: james_hunter
communicates.content: what had occurred

events.label: Straker becomes excited at hearing the account
Mrs. Straker finds John Straker dressing during the night
John Straker tells Mrs. Straker he cannot sleep and will go to the stables

communicates.speaker: john_straker
communicates.content: that he could not sleep on account of his anxiety about the horses, and that he intended to walk down to the stables to see that all was well

events.label: Mrs. Straker begs John Straker to remain at home, but he leaves the house
Mrs. Straker wakes and discovers that her husband has not returned
Mrs. Straker dresses, calls the maid, and sets off for the stables
Mrs. Straker finds the stable door open, Hunter stuporous, the horse stall empty, and no sign of the trainer
The two lads are aroused from the loft
The two lads report that they heard nothing during the night

communicates.speaker: james_hunter
communicates.content: They heard nothing during the night.

events.label: Hunter remains drugged and the others search for the missing trainer and horse
The search party climbs the knoll and sees signs of a tragedy
John Straker's overcoat is found flapping from a furze-bush
The dead body of John Straker is found in a depression in the moor
Straker's head is shattered and his thigh is cut
Straker holds a blood-clotted knife and a silk cravat in self-defense
Hunter identifies the cravat as belonging to the stranger
Hunter states that the stranger drugged his curried mutton while standing at the window

communicates.speaker: james_hunter
communicates.content: the same stranger had, while standing at the window, drugged his curried mutton, and so deprived the stables of their watchman

events.label: The missing horse is confirmed to have been present in the hollow during the struggle
The horse disappears despite a reward and the alertness of the gypsies
Analysis shows powdered opium in the remains of the horse's supper
Holmes recapitulates the police actions in the case

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I shall now recapitulate what the police have done in the matter.

events.label: Inspector Gregory arrests Fitzroy Simpson
Fitzroy Simpson is identified by name
Fitzroy Simpson's betting-book shows registered bets against the favourite
Fitzroy Simpson speaks after arrest about coming to Dartmoor to seek information

communicates.speaker: fitzroy_simpson
communicates.content: I had come down to Dartmoor in the hope of getting some information about the King's Pyland horses, and also about Desborough, the second favourite, which was in charge of Silas Brown at the Mapleton stables.

events.label: Fitzroy Simpson denies sinister intent and says he wanted first-hand information

communicates.speaker: fitzroy_simpson
communicates.content: I had no sinister designs, and had simply wished to obtain first-hand information.

events.label: Fitzroy Simpson is confronted with the cravat and turns pale
Fitzroy Simpson's wet clothing and stick are noted as matching the storm and possible weapon
Police theory is stated that Fitzroy Simpson drugged the lad and took the horse

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The police imagine that Fitzroy Simpson drugged the lad, obtained a duplicate key, opened the stable door, took out the horse, put on the bridle, led the horse away over the moor, was met or overtaken by the trainer, fought with him, beat out the trainer's brains with his heavy stick, and then either hid the horse or the horse bolted.

events.label: Holmes says he will test the matter on the spot

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I shall very quickly test the matter when I am once upon the spot.

events.label: Holmes, Watson, Colonel Ross, and Inspector Gregory arrive at Tavistock by evening
Colonel Ross greets Holmes and says he wants to avenge Straker and recover his horse

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I am delighted that you have come down, Mr. Holmes. The Inspector here has done all that could possibly be suggested, but I wish to leave no stone unturned in trying to avenge poor Straker and in recovering my horse.

events.label: Holmes asks whether there are fresh developments

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have there been any fresh developments?

events.label: Inspector Gregory says that little progress has been made

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: We have made very little progress.

events.label: The group drives through Tavistock in an open carriage
Inspector Gregory discusses his case while Holmes asks questions and interjects
Gregory states that Fitzroy Simpson is the likely suspect

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: The net is drawn pretty close round Fitzroy Simpson, and I believe myself that he is our man. At the same time I recognise that the evidence is purely circumstantial, and that some new development may upset it.

events.label: Holmes asks about Straker's knife

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: How about Straker's knife?

events.label: Gregory says that Straker wounded himself in his fall

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: We have quite come to the conclusion that he wounded himself in his fall.

events.label: Watson suggests that Straker wounded himself in his fall

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: My friend Dr. Watson made that suggestion to me as we came down. If so, it would tell against this man Simpson.

events.label: Gregory says Simpson has no knife and no wound and is strongly suspected

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Undoubtedly. He has neither a knife nor any sign of a wound. The evidence against him is certainly very strong. He had a great interest in the disappearance of the favourite. He lies under suspicion of having poisoned the stable-boy, he was undoubtedly out in the storm, he was armed with a heavy stick, and his cravat was found in the dead man's hand. I really think we have enough to go before a jury.

events.label: Holmes rejects Gregory's case against Simpson and raises objections

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: A clever counsel would tear it all to rags. Why should he take the horse out of the stable? If he wished to injure it why could he not do it there? Has a duplicate key been found in his possession? What chemist sold him the powdered opium? Above all, where could he, a stranger to the district, hide a horse, and such a horse as this? What is his own explanation as to the paper which he wished the maid to give to the stable-boy?

events.label: Gregory says Simpson claimed the paper was a ten-pound note and that one was found in his purse

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: He says that it was a ten-pound note. One was found in his purse.

events.label: Gregory says Simpson is not a stranger to Tavistock and had lodged there twice

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: But your other difficulties are not so formidable as they seem. He is not a stranger to the district. He has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer.

events.label: Gregory says the opium probably came from London, the key was thrown away, and the horse may be in a pit or old mine

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: The opium was probably brought from London. The key, having served its purpose, would be hurled away. The horse may be at the bottom of one of the pits or old mines upon the moor.

events.label: The inspector says the cravat belongs to Simpson and that Simpson lost it

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: He acknowledges that it is his, and declares that he had lost it.

events.label: A new element is introduced into the case
Holmes pricks up his ears
The police find traces of gypsies camping near the murder scene
The inspector says the gypsies were gone on Tuesday

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: On Tuesday they were gone.

events.label: The inspector proposes that Simpson may have led the horse to the gypsies

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Now, presuming that there was some understanding between Simpson and these gypsies, might he not have been leading the horse to them when he was overtaken, and may they not have him now?

events.label: Holmes agrees that the possibility exists

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is certainly possible.

events.label: The police scour the moor for the gypsies and examine stables and out-houses around Tavistock
Holmes asks about the nearby training-stable

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is another training-stable quite close, I understand?

events.label: The inspector says the nearby stable is a factor and notes its owners' interest in the favourite's disappearance

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Yes, and that is a factor which we must certainly not neglect. As Desborough, their horse, was second in the betting, they had an interest in the disappearance of the favourite. Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event, and he was no friend to poor Straker. We have, however, examined the stables, and there is nothing to connect him with the affair.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Simpson is connected with the Mapleton stables

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And nothing to connect this man Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables?

events.label: The inspector says there is nothing at all to connect Simpson with Mapleton

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Nothing at all.

events.label: The carriage stops at the villa by the road
The party arrives at the villa and Holmes remains in the carriage until roused
Holmes explains that he had been day-dreaming

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Excuse me. I was day-dreaming.

events.label: Watson notes Holmes's excitement and inferred clue-hunting
Gregory asks Holmes whether he would rather go to the crime scene

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Perhaps you would prefer at once to go on to the scene of the crime, Mr. Holmes?

events.label: Holmes says he prefers to stay and ask details

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I think that I should prefer to stay here a little and go into one or two questions of detail. Straker was brought back here, I presume? He has been in your service some years, Colonel Ross? I presume that you made an inventory of what he had in his pockets at the time of his death, Inspector? I should be very glad.

events.label: Gregory says Straker lies upstairs, the inquest is tomorrow, and he has the pocket contents in the sitting-room

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Yes; he lies upstairs. The inquest is to-morrow. I have the things themselves in the sitting-room, if you would care to see them.

events.label: The Inspector unlocks a tin box and lays Straker's pocket contents out on the table
Holmes examines the knife closely
Holmes states that the knife has blood-stains and was found in the dead man's grasp

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I presume, as I see blood-stains upon it, that it is the one which was found in the dead man's grasp. Watson, this knife is surely in your line?

events.label: Watson identifies the knife as a cataract knife

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: It is what we call a cataract knife.

events.label: Holmes comments on the knife's delicacy and awkwardness for travel
The Inspector states that the cork tip was found beside the body

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: The tip was guarded by a disk of cork which we found beside his body.

events.label: The Inspector reports Mrs. Straker's account of the knife

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: His wife tells us that the knife had lain upon the dressing-table, and that he had picked it up as he left the room. It was a poor weapon, but perhaps the best that he could lay his hands on at the moment.

events.label: Holmes asks about the papers

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Very possible. How about these papers?

events.label: The Inspector identifies the papers

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Three of them are receipted hay-dealers' accounts. One of them is a letter of instructions from Colonel Ross. This other is a milliner's account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire.

events.label: The Inspector reports Mrs. Straker's statement about Derbyshire

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Mrs. Straker tells us that Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's and that occasionally his letters were addressed here.

events.label: Holmes remarks on Derbyshire's expensive tastes and the cost of the costume

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes. Twenty-two guineas is rather heavy for a single costume.

events.label: Holmes and the others go down to the scene of the crime
Mrs. Straker steps forward and grips the Inspector's sleeve
Mrs. Straker appears haggard and eager
Mrs. Straker asks whether the missing things have been found

communicates.speaker: mrs_straker
communicates.content: Have you got them? Have you found them?

events.label: The Inspector says Holmes has come from London to help

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: No, Mrs. Straker. But Mr. Holmes here has come from London to help us, and we shall do all that is possible.

events.label: Holmes asks Mrs. Straker whether he met her in Plymouth

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Surely I met you in Plymouth at a garden-party some little time ago, Mrs. Straker?

events.label: Mrs. Straker denies Holmes's identification

communicates.speaker: mrs_straker
communicates.content: No, sir; you are mistaken.

events.label: Holmes claims he recognized Mrs. Straker by her costume

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Dear me! Why, I could have sworn to it. You wore a costume of dove-coloured silk with ostrich-feather trimming.

events.label: Mrs. Straker denies owning such a dress

communicates.speaker: mrs_straker
communicates.content: I never had such a dress, sir.

events.label: Holmes accepts the denial and follows the Inspector outside
Holmes and the others reach the hollow where the body was found
Holmes comments on the lack of wind

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There was no wind that night, I understand.

events.label: The Inspector states that there was heavy rain

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: None; but very heavy rain.

events.label: Holmes says the overcoat was placed on the furze-bush

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.

events.label: The Inspector says the overcoat was laid across the bush

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: Yes, it was laid across the bush.

events.label: Holmes notes the trampled ground

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You fill me with interest, I perceive that the ground has been trampled up a good deal. No doubt many feet have been here since Monday night.

events.label: The Inspector states that matting was laid at the side and everyone stood on it

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: A piece of matting has been laid here at the side, and we have all stood upon that.

events.label: The Inspector presents the boot, shoe, and horseshoe in a bag

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: In this bag I have one of the boots which Straker wore, one of Fitzroy Simpson's shoes, and a cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze.

events.label: Holmes praises the Inspector and takes the bag
Holmes studies the trampled mud
Holmes notices a half-burned wax vesta in the mud
Inspector finds the hidden object in the mud
Inspector compares the boots with marks on the ground
Inspector climbs to the rim of the hollow and searches the ferns and bushes
Inspector reports that no more tracks are present

communicates.speaker: inspector_gregory
communicates.content: there are no more tracks; I have examined the ground very carefully for a hundred yards in each direction

events.label: Holmes rises and says he will walk over the moor and pocket the horseshoe

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I should not have the impertinence to do it again after what you say. But I should like to take a little walk over the moor before it grows dark, that I may know my ground to-morrow, and I think that I shall put this horseshoe into my pocket for luck.

events.label: Colonel Ross invites the Inspector to return with him and asks advice about the Cup entry

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I wish you would come back with me, Inspector. There are several points on which I should like your advice, and especially as to whether we do not owe it to the public to remove our horse's name from the entries for the Cup.

events.label: Holmes tells Colonel Ross to let the horse's name stand

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Certainly not. I should let the name stand.

events.label: Colonel Ross thanks Holmes and says they will be at Straker's house

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I am very glad to have had your opinion, sir. You will find us at poor Straker's house when you have finished your walk, and we can drive together into Tavistock.

events.label: Colonel Ross and the Inspector turn back while Holmes and Watson walk across the moor
Holmes explains his hypothesis about the horse's destination

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It's this way, Watson. We may leave the question of who killed John Straker for the instant, and confine ourselves to finding out what has become of the horse. Now, supposing that he broke away during or after the tragedy, where could he have gone to? The horse is a very gregarious creature. If left to himself his instincts would have been either to return to King's Pyland or go over to Mapleton. Why should he run wild upon the moor? He would surely have been seen by now. And why should gypsies kidnap him? These people always clear out when they hear of trouble, for they do not wish to be pestered by the police. They could not hope to sell such a horse. They would run a great risk and gain nothing by taking him. Surely that is clear. Where is he, then? I have already said that he must have gone to King's Pyland or to Mapleton. He is not at King's Pyland. Therefore he is at Mapleton. Let us take that as a working hypothesis and see what it leads us to. This part of the moor, as the Inspector remarked, is very hard and dry. But it falls away towards Mapleton, and you can see from here that there is a long hollow over yonder, which must have been very wet on Monday night. If our supposition is correct, then the horse must have crossed that, and there is the point where we should look for his tracks.

events.label: Holmes and Watson reach the hollow
Holmes and Watson split up to inspect the ground
Holmes discovers a horse track and fits a shoe to the impression
Holmes comments on imagination and Gregory

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: See the value of imagination. It is the one quality which Gregory lacks. We imagined what might have happened, acted upon the supposition, and find ourselves justified. Let us proceed.

events.label: Holmes and Watson cross the marshy ground and follow the tracks
Holmes finds the tracks near Mapleton
A man's track appears beside the horse's track
Watson remarks that the horse had been alone before

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: The horse was alone before.

events.label: The double track turns toward King's Pyland
Holmes and Watson follow the returning track
The track ends at the Mapleton stables
Holmes questions the groom at the stables

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I only wished to ask a question. Should I be too early to see your master, Mr. Silas Brown, if I were to call at five o'clock to-morrow morning?

events.label: The groom identifies Silas Brown as being present

communicates.speaker: stable_lad
communicates.content: Bless you, sir, if any one is about he will be, for he is always the first stirring. But here he is, sir, to answer your questions for himself. No, sir, no; it is as much as my place is worth to let him see me touch your money. Afterwards, if you like.

events.label: Silas Brown confronts Holmes and orders them away

communicates.speaker: silas_brown
communicates.content: What's this, Dawson! No gossiping! Go about your business! And you, what the devil do you want here?

events.label: Holmes whispers to Silas Brown and gets an angry reaction

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Ten minutes' talk with you, my good sir.

events.label: Holmes and Silas Brown speak in Brown's parlour
Holmes and Silas Brown reappear after twenty minutes
Holmes confronts Silas Brown and warns against mistakes or tricks

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There must be no mistake. No, don't. I shall write to you about it. No tricks, now, or—

events.label: Holmes and Watson set off for King's Pyland
Holmes describes Silas Brown's actions on the morning of the horse's disappearance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: He tried to bluster out of it, but I described to him so exactly what his actions had been upon that morning that he is convinced that I was watching him. Of course you observed the peculiarly square toes in the impressions, and that his own boots exactly corresponded to them. Again, of course no subordinate would have dared to do such a thing. I described to him how, when according to his custom he was the first down, he perceived a strange horse wandering over the moor. How he went out to it, and his astonishment at recognising, from the white forehead which has given the favourite its name, that chance had put in his power the only horse which could beat the one upon which he had put his money. Then I described how his first impulse had been to lead him back to King's Pyland, and how the devil had shown him how he could hide the horse until the race was over, and how he had led it back and concealed it at Mapleton. When I told him every detail he gave it up and thought only of saving his own skin.

events.label: Holmes says Silas Brown will guard the horse to obtain mercy

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Oh, an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge. My dear fellow, he will guard it as the apple of his eye. He knows that his only hope of mercy is to produce it safe.

events.label: Holmes says Colonel Ross will not be told about the horse and that he will use his own methods

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The matter does not rest with Colonel Ross. I follow my own methods, and tell as much or as little as I choose. That is the advantage of being unofficial. I don't know whether you observed it, Watson, but the Colonel's manner has been just a trifle cavalier to me. I am inclined now to have a little amusement at his expense. Say nothing to him about the horse. And of course this is all quite a minor point compared to the question of who killed John Straker. On the contrary, we both go back to London by the night train.

events.label: Holmes and Watson return to the trainer's house and find Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory waiting in the parlour
Holmes says he and Watson will return to town by the night-express

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My friend and I return to town by the night-express.

events.label: Holmes asks for a photograph of John Straker

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Might I ask for a photograph of Mr. John Straker?

events.label: Holmes asks Gregory to wait while he questions the maid

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If I might ask you to wait here for an instant, I have a question which I should like to put to the maid.

events.label: Colonel Ross says he is disappointed in Holmes and sees no progress

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I must say that I am rather disappointed in our London consultant. I do not see that we are any further than when he came.

events.label: Watson says Holmes has assured them the horse will run

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: At least you have his assurance that your horse will run.

events.label: Colonel Ross says he would prefer to have the horse

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I should prefer to have the horse.

events.label: Holmes announces he is ready for Tavistock

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Now, gentlemen, I am quite ready for Tavistock.

events.label: A stable-lad holds open the carriage door for the party
Holmes questions the stable-lad about the sheep in the paddock

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have a few sheep in the paddock. Who attends to them? Have you noticed anything amiss with them of late?

events.label: The stable-lad says three sheep have gone lame

communicates.speaker: stable_lad
communicates.content: Well, sir, not of much account; but three of them have gone lame, sir.

events.label: Holmes praises the observation and orders the coach to drive on

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: A long shot, Watson; a very long shot. Gregory, let me recommend to your attention this singular epidemic among the sheep. Drive on, coachman!

events.label: Holmes points Gregory to the dog's silence in the night-time

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Exceedingly so. To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.

events.label: Holmes and Watson travel by train to Winchester for the Wessex Cup race
Colonel Ross meets Holmes and Watson outside the station and drives them to the course
Colonel Ross says he has not seen his horse

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I have seen nothing of my horse.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Colonel Ross would recognize Silver Blaze

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I suppose that you would know him when you saw him?

events.label: Holmes asks about the betting and learns the odds have shortened

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: How is the betting?

events.label: Holmes remarks that somebody knows something

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Hum! Somebody knows something, that is clear.

events.label: The race card lists the Wessex Plate entries
The Colonel says he scratched the other horse and staked everything on Holmes's word

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: We scratched our other one, and put all hopes on your word.

events.label: The ring announces odds on Silver Blaze

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Five to four against Silver Blaze! Five to fifteen against Desborough! Five to four on the field!

events.label: The narrator announces that all six horses are up

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: There are the numbers up. They are all six there.

events.label: The Colonel reacts in agitation and says his horse is running

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: Then my horse is running. But I don't see him. My colours have not passed.

events.label: A bay horse with the Colonel's colors emerges from the weighing enclosure
The Colonel denies that the bay horse is his

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: That's not my horse. That beast has not a white hair upon its body. What is this that you have done, Mr. Holmes?

events.label: Holmes tells the Colonel to wait and see how the horse gets on

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Well, well, let us see how he gets on.

events.label: Holmes watches the race through the field-glass
Holmes exclaims that the start is excellent

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Capital! An excellent start!

events.label: Holmes points out the horses coming round the curve

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There they are, coming round the curve!

events.label: The horses race up the straight
The Colonel says it is his race and asks Holmes to end the mystery

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: It's my race, anyhow. I confess that I can make neither head nor tail of it. Don't you think that you have kept up your mystery long enough, Mr. Holmes?

events.label: Holmes leads the Colonel and Watson to the weighing enclosure to see the horse
Holmes instructs them to wash the horse's face and leg in spirits of wine

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have only to wash his face and his leg in spirits of wine, and you will find that he is the same old Silver Blaze as ever.

events.label: Holmes says he found the horse in the hands of a faker and ran him as he was sent over

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I found him in the hands of a faker, and took the liberty of running him just as he was sent over.

events.label: The Colonel thanks Holmes for recovering the horse and asks him to find Straker's murderer

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: My dear sir, you have done wonders. The horse looks very fit and well. It never went better in its life. I owe you a thousand apologies for having doubted your ability. You have done me a great service by recovering my horse. You would do me a greater still if you could lay your hands on the murderer of John Straker.

events.label: Holmes says he has found Straker's murderer

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have done so.

events.label: The Colonel angrily objects to Holmes's remark

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: I quite recognise that I am under obligations to you, Mr. Holmes, but I must regard what you have just said as either a very bad joke or an insult.

events.label: Holmes laughs and denies associating the Colonel with the crime

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I assure you that I have not associated you with the crime, Colonel.

events.label: Holmes identifies the horse as the murderer and touches it

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The real murderer is standing immediately behind you.

events.label: Holmes says the horse acted in self-defence and postpones his explanation

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Yes, the horse. And it may lessen his guilt if I say that it was done in self-defence, and that John Straker was a man who was entirely unworthy of your confidence. But there goes the bell, and as I stand to win a little on this next race, I shall defer a lengthy explanation until a more fitting time.

events.label: Holmes and the others travel back to London while Holmes narrates the case

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The events which had occurred at the Dartmoor training-stables upon the Monday night and the means by which he had unravelled them.

events.label: Holmes states that his earlier theories were wrong

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Any theories which I had formed from the newspaper reports were entirely erroneous.

events.label: Holmes says he went to Devonshire suspecting Fitzroy Simpson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I went to Devonshire with the conviction that Fitzroy Simpson was the true culprit, although, of course, I saw that the evidence against him was by no means complete.

events.label: Holmes explains that the curried mutton suggested the truth to him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was while I was in the carriage, just as we reached the trainer's house, that the immense significance of the curried mutton occurred to me. You may remember that I was distrait, and remained sitting after you had all alighted. I was marvelling in my own mind how I could possibly have overlooked so obvious a clue.

events.label: The Colonel says he cannot yet see the point of Holmes's reasoning

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: That even now I cannot see how it helps us.

events.label: Holmes explains how opium in curry could be detected or disguised

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was the first link in my chain of reasoning. Powdered opium is by no means tasteless. The flavour is not disagreeable, but it is perceptible. Were it mixed with any ordinary dish the eater would undoubtedly detect it, and would probably eat no more. A curry was exactly the medium which would disguise this taste. By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson, have caused curry to be served in the trainer's family that night, and it is surely too monstrous a coincidence to suppose that he happened to come along with powdered opium upon the very night when a dish happened to be served which would disguise the flavour. That is unthinkable. Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case, and our attention centres upon Straker and his wife, the only two people who could have chosen curried mutton for supper that night. The opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy, for the others had the same for supper with no ill effects. Which of them, then, had access to that dish without the maid seeing them?

events.label: Holmes explains the significance of the dog's silence

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Before deciding that question I had grasped the significance of the silence of the dog, for one true inference invariably suggests others. The Simpson incident had shown me that a dog was kept in the stables, and yet, though some one had been in and had fetched out a horse, he had not barked enough to arouse the two lads in the loft. Obviously the midnight visitor was some one whom the dog knew well.

events.label: Holmes explains a suspected scheme to injure Silver Blaze with a knife
Holmes describes evidence from Straker's pockets and explains the motive for the crime

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And they did so. You cannot have forgotten the singular knife which was found in the dead man's hand, a knife which certainly no sane man would choose for a weapon. It was, as Dr. Watson told us, a form of knife which is used for the most delicate operations known in surgery. It was to be used for a delicate operation that night. As a man of the world, Colonel, you know that men do not carry other people's bills about in their pockets. We have most of us quite enough to do to settle our own. I at once concluded that Straker was leading a double life, and keeping a second establishment. The nature of the bill showed that there was a lady in the case, and one who had expensive tastes. Liberal as you are with your servants, one can hardly expect that they can buy twenty-guinea walking dresses for their ladies. I questioned Mrs. Straker as to the dress without her knowing it, and having satisfied myself that it had never reached her, I made a note of the milliner's address, and felt that by calling there with Straker's photograph I could easily dispose of the mythical Derbyshire.

events.label: Holmes explains that Straker led Silver Blaze out to a hollow and attempted the operation there

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: From that time on all was plain. Straker had led out the horse to a hollow where his light would be invisible. Simpson in his flight had dropped his cravat, and Straker had picked it up—with some idea, perhaps, that he might use it in securing the horse's leg. Once in the hollow, he had got behind the horse and had struck a light; but the creature frightened at the sudden glare, and with the strange instinct of animals feeling that some mischief was intended, had lashed out, and the steel shoe had struck Straker full on the forehead. He had already, in spite of the rain, taken off his overcoat in order to do his delicate task, and so, as he fell, his knife gashed his thigh. Do I make it clear?

events.label: The Colonel exclaims that something is wonderful

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: Wonderful! Wonderful!

events.label: The speaker says Colonel Ross might have been there

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: You might have been there!

events.label: The speaker explains that his final shot was a very long one

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My final shot was, I confess a very long one.

events.label: The speaker explains that Straker would have needed practice for the tendon-nicking

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It struck me that so astute a man as Straker would not undertake this delicate tendon-nicking without a little practice. What could he practice on? My eyes fell upon the sheep, and I asked a question which, rather to my surprise, showed that my surmise was correct.

events.label: The speaker says he called on the milliner in London and learned Straker was known as Derbyshire

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: When I returned to London I called upon the milliner, who had recognised Straker as an excellent customer of the name of Derbyshire, who had a very dashing wife, with a strong partiality for expensive dresses. I have no doubt that this woman had plunged him over head and ears in debt, and so led him into this miserable plot.

events.label: The Colonel asks where the horse was

communicates.speaker: colonel_ross
communicates.content: You have explained all but one thing. Where was the horse?

events.label: The speaker says the horse bolted and was cared for by a neighbour

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Ah, it bolted, and was cared for by one of your neighbours. We must have an amnesty in that direction, I think.

events.label: The speaker identifies the train location as Clapham Junction and says they will soon be in Victoria

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is Clapham Junction, if I am not mistaken, and we shall be in Victoria in less than ten minutes.

events.label: The speaker invites Colonel Ross to smoke a cigar in their rooms

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If you care to smoke a cigar in our rooms, Colonel, I shall be happy to give you any other details which might interest you.

clues.significance: Holmes used the fresh papers as source material while traveling.
Holmes inferred the train's speed from the spacing of the telegraph posts.
Mrs. Straker found John Straker's overcoat flapping from a furze-bush near the stables.
Mrs. Straker found a small knife clotted with blood in John Straker's right hand.
Mrs. Straker found a red and black silk cravat in John Straker's left hand.
Hunter identified the cravat as the one worn by the stranger who had visited the stables.
Analysis found powdered opium in the remains of the horse's supper left by the stable-lad.
Holmes used the cravat to connect Fitzroy Simpson with the murdered man.
Holmes treated Fitzroy Simpson's lead-weighted stick as a weapon that could have inflicted the trainer's injuries.
Holmes used Straker's knife to support the possibility that one assailant bore a mark from it.
Holmes used the missing bridle and the police theory to treat the horse as having been taken away from the stable.
Inspector Gregory concluded that Straker wounded himself in his fall and treated the knife issue as supporting that explanation.
Inspector Gregory used the cravat found in the dead man's hand as evidence against Fitzroy Simpson.
Holmes inferred that the opium was probably brought from London.
Gregory used the cravat as evidence that Simpson had lost it after acknowledging ownership.
Gregory inferred that a party of gypsies had encamped near the murder scene on Monday night and had gone away on Tuesday.
Gregory treated the nearby Mapleton stables and Silas Brown's betting as possible connections to the disappearance of the favourite.
Gregory produced the knife from Straker's pocket contents as part of the evidence.
Holmes inferred that the knife was a delicate cataract knife and that it was an awkward weapon for a rough expedition from its blade and pocket fit.
The Inspector established that the knife's tip had been guarded by a cork disk found beside the body.
Holmes inferred that William Derbyshire had expensive tastes from the milliner's account for a costly costume.
Holmes inferred that the overcoat had been placed on the furze-bush rather than blown there because there was no wind and heavy rain.
Holmes inferred that the trampled area had been affected by many feet because a piece of matting had been laid there and the ground was heavily disturbed.
Holmes found a half-burned wax vesta in the trampled mud, making it evidence in the investigation.
Inspector Gregory found the horseshoe buried in the mud and later Holmes took it as a luck token while using the ground and hollow as the place to search for the horse's tracks.
Holmes inferred that the horse track matched the cast horseshoe when he fit the shoe to the impression.
Holmes inferred that Silas Brown had hidden the horse at Mapleton after recognizing the white forehead and the horse that could beat the wagered animal.
Holmes inferred that the horse's whereabouts and condition were important from Colonel Ross's report and the betting movement.
Holmes inferred that opium had been mixed into curried mutton because curry could disguise its taste and the later diners were unaffected.
Holmes inferred that the horse was the murderer and had acted in self-defence.
Holmes inferred from the silence of the dog that the midnight visitor was someone the dog knew well.
Holmes inferred that Straker planned a delicate subcutaneous cut to the horse's tendons from the surgical knife found in the dead man's hand.
Holmes inferred that Straker was leading a double life and keeping a second establishment from the bill found among Straker's belongings.
Holmes inferred that Straker may have intended to use Simpson's dropped cravat to secure the horse's leg.
